rv.q: I loved every sympathy- and suspicion-shifting minute of it
Delicious archaic details include baked apples, ration books, a coked-up boiler and stockings from Gibraltar.
This is a beautifully preserved example of a country house murder mystery, a throwback to theatregoing in the thirties (minus the matinee tea-trays).
The pleasure, though, remains in marvelling that living humans might once have taken the snowbound suspects in Berkshire's Monkswell Manor Guest House seriously.
My guess is that it will run and run, unchal- lenging and unchallenged, for many years to come.
James Daly leads a superb cast in a gender and genre-inverting romp that lacks bite.
Ian Watt-Smith, the director responsible for the production's annual resuscitation, does not help to promote goose pimples and cheap thrills.
It was a pleasure to see actors as experienced as Derek Griffiths and Susan Penhaligon (as the doughty Major Metcalf and Mrs Boyle) alongside younger cast members including Danny Mac.
The real mystery of the world's longest-running theatre show is not whodunit but, in its currently mediocre state, whydoit at all?

Having negotiated decades of being just slightly unfashionable to emerge triumphantly as vintage entertainment, The Mousetrap’s liver-spotted take on the thriller is now deservedly coloured with a patina of wisdom and value.
It goes without saying that the play must also have that special something to have survived for one year, let alone over half a century.
I do recommend the Mousetrap, it was an intriguing play, how the experience certainly wasn’t all I’d hoped for.
Everything in Agatha Christie depends on the puzzle element and on her ability to spring a final surprise. This time, though, the spell doesn't work.
The Mousetrap is a brilliant play with some great acting and it will keep you on the edge of your seat until the end.

cn.t: Christie's enduring whodunnit remains a charming West End institution after 70 years, though critics find it creaky and generic. Its persistence owes more to tradition and nostalgic appeal than theatrical innovation.
